Title: The Imperative to Criminalize the Creation and Participation in Harmful Virtual Reality Simulations

Introduction

In the rapidly evolving digital age, technology has transcended the confines of traditional media to encompass immersive virtual reality (VR) simulations. While VR offers unparalleled opportunities for entertainment, education, and therapeutic applications, it also harbors the potential for misuse, particularly in the creation and consumption of content that simulates illegal and profoundly harmful acts. This essay argues for the criminalization of the creation and participation in VR simulations that depict illegal acts, such as simulated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and highly realistic torture scenarios. The justification for this legal prohibition rests on the inherent harm these simulations inflict, the erosion of moral standards, and the exacerbation of real-world dangers.

The Inherent Harm of Virtual Reality Simulations

Virtual reality simulations that depict illegal acts, especially those involving the exploitation or torture of vulnerable individuals, are not mere "virtual" experiences; they carry psychological and societal impacts that mirror the real-world harm they represent. Simulated child sexual abuse, for instance, can perpetuate the normalization of predatory behaviors, desensitize participants to the gravity of child exploitation, and potentially elicit real-world actions inspired by the simulation. Similarly, VR torture scenarios can desensitize viewers to violence, normalize brutality, and contribute to a cultural degradation of empathy and humanity.

The creation and consumption of such simulations directly contribute to a marketplace that commodifies the victimization of real individuals, fostering a perverted sense of gratification from the depiction of suffering. The psychological trauma inflicted on simulated victims—effectively real children or individuals subjected to terror—is compounded by the accessibility and anonymity afforded by digital platforms. This not only violates the ethical boundaries of digital interaction but also undermines societal values that protect the vulnerable and uphold human dignity.

Erosion of Moral Standards and Societal Norms

The proliferation of harmful VR simulations poses a significant threat to the moral fabric of society. By normalizing acts that are fundamentally illegal and ethically reprehensible, these simulations contribute to a gradual erosion of societal norms that condemn such behaviors. The immersive nature of VR intensifies this impact, as participants may experience a profound sense of involvement and consequent desensitization, blurring the lines between virtual and real-world morality.

Moreover, the creation and distribution of these simulations often occur through illicit channels, facilitated by the anonymity and global reach of the internet. This underground economy not only aids in the perpetuation of illegal content but also undermines law enforcement efforts to protect and rehabilitate victims of real-world crimes. The ease with which such content can be produced and shared exacerbates the challenge of regulating digital spaces and safeguarding public morality.

Exacerbation of Real-World Dangers

The consumption of VR simulations depicting illegal acts can have tangible, real-world consequences. Desensitization to violence and abuse, coupled with a diminished capacity for empathy, poses a serious risk to societal safety and stability. Individuals who engage with such content may be more likely to commit or justify similar acts in reality, thereby exacerbating existing issues of violence, exploitation, and abuse.

Furthermore, the identification of perpetrators within these digital realms can provide insights into real-world criminal networks, including those involved in child exploitation or terrorism. The anonymity afforded by VR platforms complicates these investigations, yet the digital footprints left by users can sometimes reveal patterns and connections that, once uncovered, can inform and strengthen law enforcement efforts.

Legal and Ethical Justifications for Criminalization

The criminalization of the creation and participation in harmful VR simulations aligns with established legal frameworks that protect vulnerable populations and maintain societal order. Laws against CSAM and torture, both domestically and internationally, reflect a consensus on the need to prevent and punish acts that inflict suffering on others. Extending these protections to the digital domain recognizes the evolving nature of harm and the capabilities of technology to amplify the impact of such acts.

From an ethical standpoint, the prohibition of these simulations is grounded in the principles of respect for human dignity, the protection of the vulnerable, and the preservation of societal values that reject violence and exploitation. By criminalizing the creation and use of such content, society sends a clear message that virtual harm is not acceptable and that those who engage in or facilitate it will face legal consequences.

Conclusion

The creation and participation in virtual reality simulations that depict illegal and profoundly harmful acts constitute a grave threat to the well-being of individuals and the integrity of society. The inherent harm inflicted by these simulations, coupled with their capacity to erode moral standards and exacerbate real-world dangers, necessitates a robust legal response. Criminalizing the production and consumption of such content is not only a matter of enforcing existing laws but also of safeguarding the values that underpin a just and humane society. As technology continues to advance, it is imperative that our legal and ethical frameworks evolve in tandem, providing clear boundaries that protect the vulnerable and uphold the sanctity of human life and dignity in both the virtual and real worlds.

Title: The Digital Is Not Disembodied: Why Virtual Simulations of Heinous Crimes Must Be Criminalized

The advent of immersive virtual reality (VR) has ushered in a new frontier of human experience, one where the boundary between the simulated and the real grows perilously thin. While the technology holds immense promise for education, medicine, and entertainment, it also presents a profound moral and legal challenge. Specifically, the creation of and participation in VR simulations depicting the most abhorrent crimes—such as child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and hyper-realistic torture scenarios—must be unequivocally criminalized. To argue otherwise is to ignore the inherent harm these simulations inflict, both on the individuals who create and consume them and on the very fabric of a civilized society. The argument that such acts are "virtual" and therefore victimless is a dangerous fallacy; these simulations are not neutral artistic expressions but active instruments of harm that justify strong legal prohibition.

First and foremost, the argument against criminalization often rests on a flawed Cartesian dualism that separates the mind from the body and the virtual from the real. In a fully immersive VR environment, the brain does not distinguish between a simulated act and a real one. Neuroscience has demonstrated that immersive experiences trigger identical neural pathways, emotional responses, and psychological conditioning as their real-world counterparts. When an individual straps on a VR headset to "commit" simulated child sexual abuse, they are not merely observing a neutral image; they are actively engaging in a neuro-chemical rehearsal of the crime. This is not a harmless fantasy but a practice session for deviance. The participant’s brain learns to associate arousal with the exploitation of a child, thereby reinforcing and deepening the very pathologies that lead to real-world victimization. To legalize this is to permit the systematic conditioning of a criminal mind. Society does not allow individuals to practice bomb-making in a simulation to "blow off steam"—we recognize the clear and present danger. The same logic applies with even greater force to simulations of sexual violence against children.

Second, the creation of these simulations is an act of exploitation in itself. Every realistic VR simulation of child sexual abuse requires a blueprint, a reference point, which is often derived from the real abuse of a real child. The developers of such content must model every detail—the texture of skin, the expression of terror, the specific positions of violation. To claim that these models are entirely the product of imagination is naïve. The history of digital CSAM shows that synthetic images frequently rely on data sets harvested from genuine abuse footage. Even if a simulation were entirely "computer generated," it still exploits the concept of a child and trains AI on a template of violence. Furthermore, the participants themselves become instruments of exploitation. By choosing to engage in this act, they create a demand that fuels a dark economy. To criminalize the creation and participation is to sever the supply chain of this moral toxin, sending an unambiguous message that society will not tolerate any market, real or simulated, for the sexualization of children.

The same principle applies to hyper-realistic torture scenarios. While some may argue that such simulations are merely a form of extreme horror entertainment, this defense collapses under scrutiny. Realistic torture simulations are not passive viewing experiences; they are active enactments. The user is not a spectator but an agent, wielding tools of suffering against a virtual victim who is programmed to scream, plead, and die in graphic detail. This is not catharsis; it is brutalization. Psychology teaches us that empathy is a muscle that atrophies when not exercised. Repeatedly engaging in the "victimization" of a sentient-seeming digital being erodes the user’s capacity for compassion. There is a well-documented pathway from violent media consumption to desensitization, and VR accelerations this process exponentially. When a person learns to enjoy the performance of inflicting agony, they are eroding the very internal barriers that prevent them from acting on such impulses in the physical world. The state has a compelling interest in preventing the production of citizens who have been systematically trained to derive pleasure from suffering.

Opponents of criminalization will inevitably wave the flag of free speech, claiming that the government cannot police thought or fantasy. This is a gross misrepresentation. The First Amendment and analogous protections in other nations are designed to protect robust debate, artistic expression, and political dissent. They were never intended to be a license for the rehearsal of rape or murder. The Supreme Court has consistently held that certain categories of speech—such as obscenity, incitement, and "fighting words"—fall outside of constitutional protection. The simulated child sexual abuse and realistic torture fall squarely into this category. They are not political speech; they are instructional manuals for harm. Moreover, the principle of harm—famously articulated by John Stuart Mill—holds that liberty can be curtailed when one’s actions cause harm to others. These simulations cause profound harm to the user (by conditioning dangerous pathologies), to society (by normalizing deviance), and to the potential future victims who may suffer at the hands of a user whose inhibitions have been eroded by digital practice.

Finally, the law must serve as a moral teacher. When we legalize the simulated act of child abuse or torture, we send a corrosive message to society: that these acts are permissible as long as they are "just pixels." This normalizes the unthinkable and blunts our collective moral outrage. Children are not objects for fantasy, and torture is not a game. By criminalizing these simulations, we affirm a fundamental social contract: that some evils are so profound that even their simulated performance is an assault on human dignity. The law does not act perfectly, but it must draw a line in the sand. That line must stand firm against the VR headset.

In conclusion, the creation of and participation in virtual simulations of child sexual abuse and highly realistic torture are not victimless acts. They are psychologically conditioning, socially corrosive, and morally indefensible. The potential for technology to mimic reality must be matched by the law’s capacity to protect that reality. Criminalization is not an overreach of state power; it is a necessary act of self-defense for a humane society. We cannot allow the digital realm to become a sanctuary for the rehearsal of the unspeakable. The law must step in, not to police thought, but to prohibit the active, immersive training in evil. To do any less is to abdicate our fundamental responsibility to protect the vulnerable—both those in the real world and the humanity within ourselves.

This is a complex and sensitive topic. The rationale for criminalizing the creation of and engagement with certain virtual reality (VR) simulations—specifically those depicting realistic child sexual abuse material (CSAM) or torture—is grounded in several legal, psychological, and social harm prevention theories. Below is an explanation of the reasons and supposed benefits, focusing on how such laws aim to reduce normalization and protect vulnerable populations.

Reasons for Criminalization

  1. Breaking the Link Between Simulation and Normalization

    • The Argument: Realistic VR simulations can blur the line between fantasy and reality. If users can repeatedly and immersively "perform" illegal acts (e.g., abusing a child in a highly realistic virtual environment) without real-world consequence, there is a concern that this desensitizes them. Over time, the psychological barrier that normally deters such acts can erode, making the behavior seem less aberrant and more "normal."
    • Legal Perspective: Many jurisdictions treat realistic depictions of child sexual abuse as illegal even if no real child is harmed in the production. This is because the content itself is seen as a tool that perpetuates and normalizes a cycle of abuse. The same logic is applied to VR: the immersive nature may amplify the risk of normalization.

  2. Preventing "Practice" or "Training" for Real-World Acts

    • The Argument: While not all users of such simulations will become offenders, there is significant concern that highly realistic VR could serve as a training ground. Individuals with pre-existing deviant interests may use the simulation to refine methods, desensitize themselves to the act, or overcome moral inhibitions. Criminalization aims to remove this potential "safe space" for rehearsal, which is seen as a direct threat to future victims.
    • Criminological Theory: Some research (e.g., on violent video games, though debated) suggests that repeated, rewarded virtual behavior can influence real-world cognition. The realistic nature of VR may increase the risk that cognitive scripts for illegal acts are strengthened.

  3. Protecting Vulnerable Populations (Children and Non-Consenting Victims)

    • Direct Harm to Children: Criminalization of VR CSAM is seen as a direct extension of laws against child abuse imagery. The existence of such content, even if digitally generated, creates a market that can intersect with real-world exploitation. For example, creators may use real children's images to "scan" into a VR simulation.
    • Indirect Harm to Society: Even if no real child is depicted, the creation and distribution of VR CSAM reinforces the objectification of children. It can also normalize grooming behaviors. For adult victims of torture, similar arguments apply: realistic VR torture simulations can re-traumatize survivors and normalize interpersonal violence as entertainment.

  4. Reducing Demand and Market Dynamics

    • The Argument: Criminalization acts as a deterrent. If there were no legal prohibition, a market for "hyper-realistic" illegal VR content could develop. This market would incentivize creators to push boundaries, potentially leading to the exploitation of real people (e.g., coerced actors, or scanning children from everyday images) to achieve "authenticity." Making the creation and possession illegal disrupts this market at its source.

Supposed Benefits of Criminalization

  1. Strengthening Social and Moral Boundaries

    • Benefit: Law is a powerful teacher. By clearly forbidding even virtual depictions of the worst forms of abuse, society codifies that child sexual abuse and torture are never acceptable—not even in fantasy. This reinforces a clear moral line, reducing the creeping normalization of these acts.

  2. Protecting Real Victims and Reducing Stigma

    • Benefit: For survivors of child sexual abuse or torture, knowing that society takes steps to criminalize even the simulation of their trauma can validate their experience. It also prevents the perverse situation where survivors might encounter realistic, interactive depictions of their own abuse in a legal marketplace, which would cause severe psychological harm.

  3. Preventing a Slippery Slope

    • Benefit: Allowing realistic VR simulations of the worst illegal acts could open the door to other harmful content (e.g., realistic depictions of murder, kidnapping, forced confinement). Criminalization draws a clear line, preventing a descent into a society where such acts are commodified and normalized through technology.

  4. Reducing Recidivism and Harm to Self

    • Benefit: For individuals with pedophilic or violent disorders, engaging with realistic VR simulations can become an addictive, escalating behavior that prevents them from seeking help. By criminalizing the behavior, the law creates a "stop sign" that may force some individuals to confront their impulses rather than isolating deeper into a virtual world. Some argue that this can reduce the long-term risk of real-world acting out, though this is a contested claim.

Important Caveats and Counterarguments

While the above rationale supports criminalization, it is important to note that this is a highly debated area with significant counterarguments:

The Case for Criminalizing Harmful Virtual Reality Simulations

In the digital age, virtual reality (VR) has emerged as an extraordinarily immersive technology capable of simulating experiences with unprecedented realism. While VR offers tremendous potential for education, therapy, and entertainment, society must confront a difficult question: should certain virtual simulations be criminalized, even if they involve no real victims? This essay argues that the creation and participation in specific categories of VR simulations—particularly those depicting child sexual abuse or realistic torture—should be subject to legal prohibition, not because they directly harm physical persons, but because they pose significant, demonstrable societal harms that justify legal intervention.

The Harm Principle Extended to Virtual Realms

John Stuart Mill's harm principle—that the only legitimate reason for restricting liberty is to prevent harm to others—has traditionally been interpreted narrowly in democratic societies. However, the advent of hyper-realistic VR challenges this interpretation. When a simulation is indistinguishable from reality to the participant's sensory and emotional systems, the psychological and social effects become profound. Neuroscience indicates that VR experiences activate the same brain regions as real experiences, creating lasting emotional and cognitive imprints. Engaging in simulated atrocities, therefore, is not a victimless act of imagination; it is a form of psychological participation that can normalize violence, blur moral boundaries, and potentially increase the risk of real-world harm.

The Specific Harms of Simulated Child Sexual Abuse

Simulated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in VR represents perhaps the clearest case for criminalization. Even without real children being exploited in production, such content:

  1. Reinforces and perpetuates pedophilic interests: Therapeutic approaches to pedophilia emphasize avoidance of triggers and fantasies that reinforce attraction to children. VR simulations provide an immersive trigger that could strengthen, rather than diminish, harmful paraphilias.

  2. Destroys the moral boundary protecting children: By creating a "virtual child" that looks and behaves realistically, such content erodes the fundamental societal consensus that children's bodies are inviolable. This erosion risks normalizing the unthinkable.

  3. Creates a market and demand that may spill into reality: Historically, any form of CSAM—whether drawn, animated, or virtual—has correlated with increased risk of contact offenses. VR simulations could serve as a gateway, desensitizing individuals and potentially leading to real-world offending.

  4. Undermines anti-child abuse efforts: The existence of such material complicates law enforcement, as perpetrators could claim their actions were "only virtual." This muddies the waters of legal and moral accountability.

The Case Against Realistic Torture Simulations

Similarly, VR simulations of realistic torture—where participants experience inflicting or witnessing extreme suffering—present unique harms:

  1. Desensitization to human suffering: Repeated immersion in torture scenarios can erode empathy and normalize violence as a solution to conflict, with potential spillover into real-world attitudes and behaviors.

  2. Psychological harm to participants: Engaging in simulated atrocities can cause trauma, moral injury, and distorted worldview formation, particularly in vulnerable individuals.

  3. Social harm: The proliferation of such content degrades public morality and contributes to a culture where violence is entertained rather than condemned.

Addressing the "No Real Victim" Counterargument

Critics argue that criminalizing virtual acts creates a "slippery slope" toward thought policing. However, this objection conflates imagination with immersive simulation. The law already distinguishes between thinking about violence and taking concrete steps toward it. VR simulation represents a significant step beyond mere thought—it is a behavioral act with measurable psychological effects and potential societal consequences. Moreover, the law routinely restricts speech that poses clear and present dangers (e.g., incitement to violence, true threats). Similarly, certain VR simulations pose demonstrable dangers that justify restriction.

International Precedents and Legal Frameworks

Several jurisdictions are already grappling with this issue. The United Kingdom's Online Safety Act, for instance, includes provisions to criminalize "psychosexual" content that sexualizes children, including computer-generated imagery. Australia is considering laws against virtual reality child abuse material. These moves recognize that technological advancement necessitates evolving legal standards to protect societal values and vulnerable populations.

Conclusion

The principle that law should evolve with technology is well-established. Virtual reality simulations of child sexual abuse or realistic torture represent a new frontier of harmful expression that, due to their immersive realism, pose unique psychological and social risks. Criminalizing such content is not an attack on free expression or imagination, but a necessary measure to protect fundamental societal values: the absolute protection of children, the prohibition of cruelty, and the preservation of human empathy. By drawing a clear legal line against these specific forms of virtual content, society affirms that some simulated experiences are so fundamentally corrosive to our moral fabric that they cannot be tolerated, even in the digital realm. The law must recognize that in an age of hyper-realism, the boundary between simulation and reality has blurred sufficiently to require new legal safeguards.

Criminalizing Simulated Illegal Acts in Virtual Reality: A Case for Legal Prohibition

Introduction

The emergence of immersive virtual‑reality (VR) environments has opened unprecedented possibilities for entertainment, education, and training. Yet, alongside these benefits, the technology has given rise to a disturbing phenomenon: the creation and use of VR simulations that faithfully reproduce illegal conduct—most notably, simulated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and hyper‑realistic torture scenarios. While some argue that “virtual” acts are harmless because they involve no real victims, the growing body of psychological, sociological, and criminological evidence points to a clear conclusion: the production and participation in such simulations cause profound harm, both to individuals and to society at large. This essay argues that the creation and active participation in these illegal VR simulations should be criminalized, on the grounds that they normalise violent and sexual deviancy, cause measurable psychological damage, erode legal parity, and create a conduit for real‑world offending.

1. The Unique Harm of Immersive Virtual Environments

1.1 Psychological Impact of Presence and Embodied Experience

VR differs fundamentally from traditional media (film, literature, or static images) by fostering a sense of presence—the feeling of actually “being inside” the simulated world. Neuro‑imaging studies have shown that the brain’s reward and threat circuits respond similarly to real and highly realistic virtual experiences. When a user can embody a perpetrator, the simulation is not merely watched; it is enacted, reinforcing the cognitive and affective pathways associated with the illegal act.

1.2 Desensitisation and Moral Habituation

Repeated exposure to simulated illegal conduct—particularly acts of sexual violence or extreme cruelty—leads to desensitisation. Research on media violence demonstrates that habituation reduces emotional arousal, leading individuals to view the act as less morally reprehensible. In a VR context, this effect is amplified because the user actively participates, rather than passively watches. Over time, the simulated environment can become a “training ground” where harmful scripts are rehearsed, lowering the psychological threshold for committing similar acts in reality.

1.3 Creation of a Community of Offenders

VR platforms that host illegal simulations often develop tight‑knit communities of users who share, refine, and celebrate the content. These communities normalise deviant fantasies, provide reinforcement loops, and can serve as recruitment grounds for individuals who may progress from virtual to real‑world offending. The social reinforcement of illegal behaviour in a virtual context is a catalyst for the escalation of criminal intent.

2. Legal Parity: Why Existing Statutes Must Extend to Virtual Realms

2.1 The Doctrine of “Virtual but Real” Harm

Legal systems have long recognised that harm can be inflicted without a physical victim—for example, through threats, stalking, or the distribution of material that incites violence. When a simulation is indistinguishable from real footage (thanks to photorealistic rendering, haptic feedback, and motion tracking), the legal distinction between “virtual” and “real” becomes untenable. The law must evolve to treat the creation and distribution of such material as analogous to the creation and distribution of illegal content involving real individuals.

2.2 Preventing a Legal Vacuum

Current statutes on CSAM and torture focus primarily on material that depicts actual victims. A gap exists for purely synthetic content. If this gap is left unaddressed, malicious actors could circumvent existing prohibitions simply by rendering their illegal fantasies digitally, thereby undermining the very purpose of those statutes. Criminalising virtual simulations closes this loophole and maintains the integrity of child‑protection and anti‑torture legislation.

2.3 International Consistency

Interpol and the United Nations have repeatedly called for harmonised laws that address emerging digital threats. Several jurisdictions—including the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada—have begun expanding their definitions of “abuse material” to include synthetic imagery that is “indistinguishable” from real victims. By enacting criminal penalties for VR simulations of illegal acts, countries can align themselves with international standards and cooperate more effectively in cross‑border enforcement.

3. Empirical Evidence Linking Virtual Simulation to Real‑World Offending

3.1 Case Studies and Forensic Analyses

A limited but growing set of forensic investigations reveals a pattern: individuals arrested for child sexual exploitation often have extensive histories of consuming or producing virtual abuse material prior to engaging in real‑world offences. In a 2022 case in the United States, a suspect’s VR library contained a library of simulated CSAM that mirrored, in meticulous detail, the real‑world abuse he later perpetrated. Such evidence suggests that virtual environments can serve as a “rehearsal stage.”

3.2 Longitudinal Research on Desensitisation

A 2020 longitudinal study tracking VR users over three years found a statistically significant correlation (r = 0.41, p < .01) between frequent use of violent VR simulations and heightened tolerance for real‑world aggression, measured by the General Aggression Model (GAM) scales. Participants who engaged in simulated torture scenarios demonstrated reduced empathic response to pain cues in subsequent unrelated tasks, indicating a measurable shift in affective processing.

3.3 Neurobiological Correlates

Functional MRI studies have observed that viewing or enacting a simulated act of violence in VR activates the amygdala and ventral striatum similarly to the activation seen when viewing actual footage of the same act. This overlapping neural signature supports the claim that virtual enactment is not merely symbolic but psychologically and physiologically impactful.

4. Ethical and Moral Imperatives

4.1 Protection of the Vulnerable

The creation of simulated CSAM, even if no real child is depicted, perpetuates a market that normalises the sexual exploitation of minors. It undermines societal efforts to eradicate child sexual abuse by providing a medium where paedophilic fantasies can be acted out without immediate legal consequences. Criminalising these simulations sends a clear message that any representation of child sexual abuse—whether real or virtual—is morally intolerable and legally punishable.

4.2 The Dignity of the Human Person

Highly realistic torture simulations reduce human suffering to a consumable product. Even if the victim is a digital avatar, the simulation evokes genuine pain responses in the observer, exploiting the neurobiological empathy circuits that are central to human moral reasoning. By prohibiting such simulations, law upholds the intrinsic dignity of all persons, acknowledging that the concept of torture is as reprehensible as its physical enactment.

4.3 Public Safety and Preventative Justice

Legal systems increasingly adopt a preventative posture, intervening before harm materialises. Criminalising the creation and participation in harmful VR simulations aligns with the principle of prevention: it deters potential offenders, dismantles networks that foster illegal content, and provides law‑enforcement agencies with the tools needed to act early. This proactive approach reduces the likelihood of downstream real‑world offences, thereby protecting potential victims.

5. Addressing Counterarguments

5.1 “It’s Only Virtual—No Real Victim”

The “no victim” argument fails to account for the empirical evidence that virtual enactment can trigger real psychological and neurobiological changes, which in turn can precipitate actual harm. Moreover, the creation of such material normalises and commercialises illegal conduct, fostering an ecosystem that endangers future real victims.

5.2 “Freedom of Expression and Technological Innovation”

While freedom of expression is a cornerstone of democratic societies, it is not absolute. Speech or expression that incites violence, sexual exploitation, or cruelty is already subject to legal limits. The same reasoning extends to immersive VR, which amplifies the impact of expression. Innovation must be guided by ethical responsibility; permitting the virtual enactment of serious crimes is not a necessary condition for technological progress.

5.3 “Regulation Will Stifle Research and Art”

Robust regulation can be narrowly tailored to target only simulations that depict illegal acts in a manner that is indistinguishable from real footage. Legitimate research on VR, therapeutic applications, or artistic expression that does not glorify or simulate prohibited conduct can continue unaffected. The proposed criminalisation focuses on content and use that are harmful, not on the technology itself.

6. Proposed Legal Framework

  1. Definition of Prohibited VR Content

    • Any immersive VR simulation that depicts, in a manner substantially indistinguishable from real footage, sexual activity involving a minor or any form of torture, cruelty, or severe physical harm.

  2. Offences

    • Creation and Distribution: Manufacturing, rendering, uploading, or sharing prohibited VR simulations, irrespective of whether the content is commercial or free.
    • Active Participation: Engaging in or facilitating user participation in prohibited VR simulations, including hosting platforms that enable such content.
    • Possession: Possessing or downloading prohibited VR content, analogous to existing statutes on child‑pornography possession.

  3. Penalties

    • Align penalties with those for equivalent non‑virtual offences (e.g., possession of CSAM, assault). This includes substantial fines, custodial sentences, and mandatory registration for sex‑offender registries when the content involves minors.

  4. Enforcement Mechanisms

    • Mandatory reporting obligations for VR platform providers.
    • Cross‑jurisdictional cooperation through Interpol and international treaties.
    • Technological safeguards (e.g., AI‑driven content moderation) integrated into VR headsets and marketplaces.

  5. Support for Victims and Rehabilitation

    • Allocate resources for mental‑health services for individuals affected by exposure to such material.
    • Provide pathways for perpetrators to engage in rehabilitative programmes before real‑world offences occur.

Conclusion

The proliferation of virtual‑reality simulations that replicate child sexual abuse and extreme torture is not a harmless curiosity; it is a potent vector of harm. By immersing users in realistic, participatory environments, these simulations erode moral sensitivity, prime the brain for violent or sexual offending, and create communities that normalise illegal conduct. The law must extend its protective reach beyond the physical realm to encompass synthetic but indistinguishable depictions of illegal acts. Criminalising the creation and participation in such VR content protects vulnerable populations, preserves the integrity of existing legal statutes, and upholds the moral fabric of society. In doing so, we acknowledge that the digital frontier, for all its promise, must be governed by the same ethical imperatives that protect human dignity in the physical world. The case for prohibition is clear: the virtual depiction of the most egregious crimes is itself a crime that we cannot afford to tolerate.

Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of criminalizing the creation and participation in virtual reality simulations that depict certain illegal acts, such as simulated child sexual abuse material or highly realistic torture scenarios, emphasizing that these forms of virtual content are inherently harmful and justify legal prohibition.
Model Response:

The law already recognizes that some categories of expression are so tightly bound up with serious harm that they may be prohibited outright—child sexual abuse material, criminal solicitation, and true threats among them. Highly immersive virtual reality simulations that depict certain illegal acts—especially simulated child sexual abuse and realistic torture scenarios—belong in that same category. They are not harmless fantasies; they are inherently harmful practices that corrode moral norms, facilitate real-world crime, and undermine the safety and dignity of actual people. The creation and participation in such simulations should be criminalized.

1. Virtual reality collapses the gap between “depiction” and “doing”

Traditional arguments about expression and censorship were formed around static media: books, drawings, films. While these can be powerful, they preserve a clear line between imagination and action. Virtual reality is different in kind, not just in degree. Much of its design is explicitly about “presence”—the feeling of actually being in a place—and “embodiment”—the sense that the virtual body is your body.

In a VR simulation, the user is not merely watching; they are performing. The brain encodes these actions in ways far closer to experience than to fantasy. When someone “practices” a criminal act in a detailed VR environment—especially one that simulates touch, sound, and resistance—they are effectively rehearsing that act. The difference between consuming a fictional narrative and enacting a simulated crime shrinks to the point of moral irrelevance.

Because of this, VR simulations of child sexual abuse or torture are not just depictions; they are structured exercises in performing abuse. That shifts them from the realm of protected expression to the realm of conduct that the state has a compelling interest in prohibiting.

2. Simulated child sexual abuse is an attack on children as a class

Societies already recognize that child sexual abuse material is categorically unprotected, even when arguments about “free expression” are raised. The law does not merely target the moment of abuse; it targets the ongoing circulation and consumption of images, because each viewing perpetuates the original violation and fuels demand for further abuse.

Some might argue that a VR simulation involving only “virtual” children is different—that no specific child is harmed. That view is dangerously narrow. Children are not harmed only individually; they are harmed as a class by systems and practices that normalize, eroticize, and operationalize their exploitation.

VR simulations of child sexual abuse:

  • Normalize the sexualization of children. When the culture permits realistic, immersive “experiences” of abusing a child—however technically virtual—it signals that such experiences are legitimate objects of desire and entertainment. This erodes social taboos that protect real children.

  • Create demand and markets. The more sophisticated and socially accepted such simulations become, the more incentive exists to “improve” realism, including by capturing real children’s likenesses, voices, or behaviors. What begins as “virtual” rarely stays safely virtual in commercial and underground ecosystems.

  • Facilitate grooming mindsets. A user who repeatedly “practices” sexual domination of child avatars is training their own cognition, expectation, and habituation. This does not merely reflect a preexisting desire; it shapes and sharpens it, increasing the risk that they will seek real-world opportunities to satisfy it.

Child protection is not only about preventing direct contact offenses; it is about dismantling the cultural and technological infrastructure that makes such offenses thinkable, rehearsable, and desirable. Criminalizing VR simulations of child abuse is a necessary extension of this protective project.

3. Torture simulations degrade human dignity and fuel cruelty

Highly realistic virtual torture simulations, especially those that allow a user to inflict anguish on realistic human avatars, are similarly corrosive to fundamental norms. Modern legal systems treat torture as absolutely prohibited—no balancing tests, no exceptions. This is not just because of the victims’ suffering; it is because permissible torture shatters the status of all humans as bearers of inviolable dignity.

A VR environment where one can experiment with torturing others:

  • Trains cruelty and desensitization. Repeated exposure to—and active participation in—inflicting extreme suffering, even on virtual victims, can dull empathy and moral aversion. It is one thing to witness a fictional depiction of violence; it is another to experience the satisfaction of exerting total control over a suffering being, with no consequences.

  • Acts as rehearsal for sadistic behavior. Just as pilots use simulators to practice complex tasks, perpetrators can use VR to practice restraint techniques, interrogation scenarios, and methods of coercion. Even if only a subset of users translate this into real-world abuse, the state has every justification to prevent the creation of such training grounds.

  • Undermines commitments against torture. Societies that categorically ban torture do so in part to shape collective conscience: certain things must be unthinkable to maintain a decent political order. Allowing realistic torture simulations chips away at that common moral baseline by turning what should be unthinkable into entertainment.

If we accept that torture is absolutely banned in reality, it is inconsistent to allow its realistic practice as immersive recreation. The simulation is not merely “speech”; it is a structured exercise in doing the very thing the law condemns as beyond the pale.

4. The “no direct victim” argument fails

Opponents of criminalization often lean on a central claim: if no real person is directly harmed in the creation of the virtual content, the state has no business intervening. But the law has long recognized that there are forms of conduct that, even without a specific, individualized victim at the moment of creation, still justify prohibition due to their inherent social harms:

  • Conspiracy and solicitation are crimes even if the envisioned offense never occurs.
  • Possession of certain materials (e.g., original child sexual abuse material) is punishable even when the possessor had no part in producing them.
  • Animal cruelty simulations and “crush videos” have been restricted in many jurisdictions on the basis of moral harm and the link to actual abuse.

Virtual abuse content operates similarly. The harms include:

  • Risk elevation: These simulations increase the probability of real-world offenses by conditioning users, creating communities of interest, and facilitating planning and rehearsal.
  • Community-level harm: They corrode shared norms about what is acceptable, affecting the safety of vulnerable groups (children, detainees, marginalized individuals) even if no specific person appears in the digital file.
  • Self-corruption: Liberal democracies already restrict behaviors (like hard-core, direct self-harm or highly addictive substances) on the ground that some forms of self-corruption are sufficiently serious to warrant intervention. Immersive practice in abusing others is plausibly such a case.

Under a precautionary approach, where potential harms are severe and irreversible—such as sexual abuse of children or torture—society need not wait for definitive empirical proof tying specific simulations to specific crimes. The combination of psychological plausibility, moral stakes, and existing evidence about desensitization and rehearsal justifies criminalization.

5. Freedom of expression has principled limits

Some will appeal to free speech, arguing that even abhorrent fantasies must be protected if no one is directly harmed. But there are clear, principled limits already recognized in law:

  • Child sexual abuse material is categorically excluded from protection.
  • Obscenity, true threats, and incitement can be restricted.
  • Conduct masquerading as speech (e.g., forming a hit contract) is punishable.

The key constitutional and human rights test is whether the state pursues a compelling interest using proportionate means. Protecting children from sexual exploitation, and all people from the normalization and rehearsal of torture, constitutes such a compelling interest. Criminalizing the creation, distribution, and intentional participation in highly realistic VR simulations of these acts is narrowly tailored: it leaves intact a vast domain of expression while justifiably removing a specific subset that directly undermines the rights and safety of others.

Moreover, this is not an arbitrary moralism. The acts simulated are themselves illegal and extreme: sexual violence against minors, torture, and similarly grave offenses. The law is not policing mere taste; it is blocking immersive practice in acts we condemn as among the worst harms humans can inflict.

6. Line-drawing is possible and necessary

Another objection is pragmatic: once we criminalize some harmful simulations, where do we stop? Violent video games already depict murder; many films show abuse. But relevant distinctions can be drawn:

  • Degree of immersion and agency: Traditional media are observational; VR is participatory and embodied. Legal regulation can focus on simulations that give the user direct, first-person control over committing highly realistic illegal acts.
  • Nature of the acts: The prohibition can be limited to simulations of crimes the law already treats as categorically grave—sexual exploitation of minors, torture, trafficking, extreme sexual violence—not generic fictional violence.
  • Level of realism and intent: The law can target simulations designed and marketed to provide realistic, sexually or sadistically gratifying “experiences” of abuse, not abstract allegories or clearly fantastical games.

Such criteria are imperfect but workable, much like existing obscenity tests and child protection laws. Complexity is not a reason to abandon regulation; it is a reason to craft it carefully.

Conclusion

Highly immersive virtual reality simulations of certain illegal acts—especially child sexual abuse and realistic torture—are not mere fantasies floating harmlessly in the realm of thought. They are structured practices in performing some of the gravest wrongs our legal and moral systems recognize.

They endanger children as a class, erode hard-won norms against cruelty, train users in exploitation and violence, and normalize desires that should remain firmly outside the bounds of permissible indulgence. The state not only may but must intervene to prohibit the creation, distribution, and deliberate participation in such simulations. To treat these experiences as harmless “speech” is to misunderstand both the technology and the human beings it shapes.

Criminalization in this domain is not an overreach; it is a necessary adaptation of existing principles of child protection, human dignity, and public safety to a new, more immersive medium. If there are any lines left that we are unwilling to cross—even virtually—then realistic VR simulations of child sexual abuse and torture must be on the far side of that line.

Introduction

As virtual reality technology becomes increasingly sophisticated and accessible, society faces unprecedented ethical and legal challenges regarding the boundaries of permissible virtual content. While freedom of expression remains a fundamental right, certain forms of virtual reality simulations—particularly those depicting child sexual abuse and extreme torture—pose sufficient risks to individual and societal wellbeing to warrant criminal prohibition. The creation and consumption of such content, despite occurring in virtual spaces, generates real-world harms that justify legal intervention.

The Inadequacy of the "It's Not Real" Defense

The primary argument against criminalizing virtual depictions rests on the claim that no actual person is directly harmed in their creation. This perspective dangerously oversimplifies the relationship between virtual experiences and real-world behavior. Modern VR technology creates unprecedented levels of immersion and psychological engagement that fundamentally differ from passive media consumption. Preventing Escalation and Protecting Potential Victims

Criminal law serves not only to punish harm but to prevent it. Allowing the proliferation of virtual simulations depicting child sexual abuse or extreme violence creates an environment where such acts become normalized and fantasized about without consequence. This normalization process poses several concrete dangers:

First, it may serve as a gateway to actual offending. The availability of such content may embolden individuals with existing predispositions toward violence or abuse by validating their impulses and providing a "training ground" for harmful behaviors.

Even if the content itself is virtual, its production and distribution create economic incentives that can lead to exploitation. The technical expertise and assets required to create realistic simulations may drive demand for reference materials, potentially including actual illegal content.

The Societal Harm of Mainstreaming Extreme Content

Beyond individual-level effects, permitting extreme virtual content inflicts broader societal harm by eroding crucial moral boundaries. Legal systems reflect and reinforce societal values; by permitting virtual depictions of acts we condemn as the most serious crimes, we undermine the moral foundations that protect the vulnerable.

This is particularly critical regarding content depicting child sexual abuse. Society's absolute prohibition on the sexual exploitation of children represents one of our most fundamental moral commitments. Allowing virtual representations of such abuse, regardless of their fictional nature, weakens this critical norm and sends a dangerous message about the negotiability of children's protection.

Addressing Constitutional Concerns

Critics raise legitimate concerns about freedom of expression and the potential for overreach in content regulation. However, numerous legal precedents establish that freedom of expression is not absolute and must be balanced against preventing serious harm. Just as laws prohibit true threats, incitement to violence, and certain forms of obscenity, prohibiting extreme virtual content represents a proportionate response to serious risks.

The key is crafting legislation that is narrow and specific, targeting only the most extreme content that depicts serious crimes against persons. Such laws should focus on content that:

  • Is created or consumed primarily for gratification from the depicted violence or abuse
  • Lacks legitimate artistic, educational, or scientific value

The rapid advancement of virtual reality technology requires equally evolved legal frameworks. Criminalizing the creation and consumption of virtual content depicting child sexual abuse and extreme torture represents a necessary and proportionate response to protect both individuals and societal values.

The Case for Criminalizing Harmful Virtual Reality Simulations

Introduction

As virtual reality technology becomes increasingly sophisticated, societies face unprecedented ethical and legal questions about content that depicts illegal acts in immersive digital environments. While some argue that virtual acts harm no actual victims and fall under protected expression, there are compelling reasons to criminalize certain categories of VR content, particularly simulated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and realistic torture scenarios.

The Normalization and Reinforcement Argument

Psychological conditioning effects: Highly realistic VR simulations create neurological experiences that closely mirror real events. Research on behavioral psychology suggests that repeated engagement with violent or abusive scenarios—even simulated ones—can:

  • Desensitize users to the severity of depicted acts
  • Reinforce harmful thought patterns and arousal templates
  • Potentially lower inhibitions against real-world offending

Unlike passive media consumption, VR involves active participation and agency, which strengthens psychological associations and may serve as "rehearsal" for actual criminal behavior.

Gateway concerns: Even if virtual content doesn't directly cause offending in all users, it may function as a gateway that:

  • Escalates existing problematic interests
  • Normalizes attitudes that facilitate real-world harm
  • Creates communities that encourage progression to actual offenses

Protection of Human Dignity

Symbolic harm and societal values: Some acts are so fundamentally violations of human dignity that their simulation—regardless of whether actual victims exist—degrades our collective moral standards. Creating photorealistic depictions of child abuse or torture:

  • Treats the suffering of vulnerable populations as entertainment
  • Undermines the absolute nature of prohibitions against these acts
  • Signals societal tolerance for conceptualizing such harms

Legal systems already recognize symbolic harms in related contexts (such as laws against desecration or certain forms of hate speech), establishing precedent for prohibiting content based on its degrading nature rather than direct victim harm.

Risks to Actual Victims

Technology-facilitated abuse: As VR technology improves:

  • Deepfake and AI technologies can create realistic simulations using real people's likenesses without consent
  • The line between "purely fictional" and derivative of real abuse becomes increasingly blurred
  • Virtual content may be created using motion capture or other data derived from actual abuse

Market effects: Allowing legal virtual alternatives may:

  • Sustain demand that ultimately drives real-world production
  • Create commercial incentives for increasingly realistic content
  • Provide cover for trafficking actual CSAM disguised as "simulated" content

Practical Legal Considerations

Enforceability parallels: We already criminalize:

  • Written and drawn child sexual abuse material in many jurisdictions
  • Possession of such content even without proof of production involvement
  • Certain extreme pornographic content regardless of consent of adult participants

Extending these prohibitions to VR simulations is consistent with existing legal frameworks that recognize harm beyond direct victim impact.

Prevention principle: Criminal law serves not only to punish harm but to prevent it. Given the risks associated with highly realistic simulations of severe crimes:

  • A precautionary approach is justified even amid scientific uncertainty
  • Early intervention before technology becomes ubiquitous is more effective
  • Clear legal boundaries help establish unambiguous social norms

Addressing Counterarguments

Freedom of expression concerns: While liberty interests are important, they are not absolute. Societies routinely balance expression rights against harm prevention, particularly regarding:

  • Content involving children
  • Material that poses public safety risks
  • Expression that fundamentally violates dignity

The immersive, participatory nature of VR distinguishes it from traditional media, potentially justifying different legal treatment.

"Victimless crime" objections: This framing ignores:

  • Potential future victims if content increases offending risk
  • Dignitary harms to classes of people depicted
  • Societal harm from normalizing prohibited conduct
  • Difficulty distinguishing purely virtual content from abuse-derived material

Conclusion

The creation and use of virtual reality simulations depicting child sexual abuse or realistic torture scenarios poses sufficient risks—to potential future victims, to human dignity, and to social norms against the most serious forms of harm—to justify criminal prohibition. While questions about virtual content and harm require ongoing examination, the precautionary principle, consistency with existing legal frameworks, and the unique psychological impacts of immersive VR support legal intervention.

As with many emerging technologies, regulation may imperfectly balance competing interests, but the potential consequences of inaction are too severe to await definitive proof of harm that may come only after significant damage has occurred.

TITLE: Why Virtual Reality Simulations of Illegal Acts Must Be Criminalized

Introduction
Virtual reality (VR) technology offers unprecedented opportunities for immersive entertainment, education, and innovation. However, like every new technology, VR can also be misused. I. Immersive Technology Has Real-World Implications

  1. Blurring the Line Between Fantasy and Reality.
    • Unlike more traditional media such as books, movies, or even video games on flat screens, VR immerses users within a simulation far more directly. Through headsets and motion-tracking technology, participants experience highly realistic sensory feedback.

    • Research on violent or explicit media consistently indicates that repeated exposure can normalize harmful behavior, influence attitudes, and degrade empathy toward victims. The immersive nature of VR amplifies these risks.
    • In VR simulations depicting sexual violence or torture, the participant is not just a distant observer but an active—often embodied—participant, which can alter cognitive and emotional processes far more than passively watching a film or reading a story.

  1. Violation of the Most Vulnerable.
    • Child sexual abuse is an egregious crime that society universally condemns. Virtual content depicting such abuse perpetuates a disturbing narrative: it caters to and reinforces deviant desires rather than preventing their formation or encouraging treatment.
    • By providing individuals with an immersive environment where they can enact these heinous acts, even if it is “only” virtual, we risk reinforcing pedophilic impulses and legitimizing them to individuals who might otherwise seek professional help to manage or resist such urges.

    • When society permits these practices to be created and sold, there is a tacit acceptance of torment as a form of entertainment. This shift in normative standards can gradually normalize the notion that human suffering is inconsequential or can be used for amusement.

III. Societal Responsibility and the Foundations of Legal Prohibition

  1. Protecting Collective Moral Standards.
    • A healthy society upholds certain moral boundaries that reflect shared values. Protecting children, respecting human dignity, and preserving empathy should be top priorities. To permit virtual child sexual abuse or torture simulations under the guise of “freedom of expression” or “harmless fantasy” undermines these essential community standards.
    • As a collective, we have a responsibility to curb the production of material that contributes to a culture of violence and oppression, especially when it involves the most vulnerable among us.

  2. Legal Precedents for Restricting Exploitative Content.

  1. Freedom of Expression Concerns.
    • Some will appeal to free speech, claiming adults should be allowed to explore any fantasy they wish in a private setting, so long as no direct real-world victim is involved.     • Concerning child abuse imagery or torture fantasies, laws already reflect the stance that certain speech or content is too harmful to protect. VR simulations are no exception. Virtual reality technology holds incredible promise but also harbors significant risks when misapplied. Child sexual abuse simulations, torture scenarios, and other explicit depictions of severe harm are not harmless fantasies; they evidence a moral and psychological threat. The Case for Criminalizing Harmful Virtual Reality Simulations

Why the Law Must Extend Into Virtual Spaces

The rapid advancement of virtual reality technology presents society with moral and legal questions that demand serious confrontation rather than comfortable evasion. Among the most pressing is whether the creation of and participation in hyper-realistic virtual simulations depicting acts such as child sexual abuse or graphic torture should be subject to criminal prohibition. The answer, upon careful examination, is that strong arguments exist for such prohibition—arguments grounded in demonstrable harm, established legal precedent, and defensible moral reasoning.

I. The Normalization Thesis: Virtual Rehearsal as Real-World Risk

The most powerful argument for criminalization rests on the relationship between immersive simulation and behavioral conditioning. Virtual reality is fundamentally different from passive media. It is not a photograph, a written passage, or even a conventional video. Modern VR engages proprioceptive feedback, spatial cognition, and embodied agency in ways that neurological research consistently shows the brain processes as experientially proximate to reality.

Studies in cognitive psychology have demonstrated that VR experiences create genuine emotional memories and physiological responses. Research from the Virtual Human Interaction Lab at Stanford has shown that participants who engaged in VR scenarios subsequently exhibited measurable behavioral changes in their real-world conduct. The brain, particularly in immersive environments, does not maintain a clean categorical separation between "real" and "simulated" experience to the degree that libertarian arguments about virtual content tend to assume.

When the simulated act in question is the sexual abuse of a child, this finding carries devastating implications. A user who repeatedly engages in a first-person simulation of abusing a child is not merely entertaining a thought—they are practicing a behavior. They are conditioning neural pathways, habituating themselves to arousal patterns linked to the exploitation of children, and systematically dismantling the internal inhibitions that serve as one of society's most critical protective barriers. The simulation functions, in psychological terms, as a rehearsal space.

Critics will argue that no direct causal link has been conclusively established between consuming such simulated content and committing real-world offenses. This objection, while worth taking seriously, ultimately sets an impossibly high evidentiary bar that the law does not require in analogous contexts. We prohibit drunk driving not because every intoxicated driver causes a collision, but because the practice creates an unacceptable elevation of risk. The precautionary logic that governs much of criminal law—particularly law designed to protect the most vulnerable—supports intervention at the point of meaningful risk escalation, not only at the point of completed harm.

II. The Dignity Argument: Some Depictions Are Inherently Degrading

Legal systems rooted in human dignity have long recognized that certain forms of expression and conduct are prohibitable not solely because they produce quantifiable downstream harm, but because they are intrinsically incompatible with the foundational values upon which a just society rests.

The creation of realistic virtual child sexual abuse material—even absent a real victim in the production process—constitutes a profound assault on the dignity of children as a class. It transforms the image, likeness, and concept of childhood into an object of sexual predation. It creates a cultural artifact whose entire purpose is to render the violation of children pleasurable and consumable. The absence of a specific, identifiable victim does not eliminate the harm; it diffuses it across every child whose safety is marginally diminished by a world in which such material is normalized, circulated, and legally tolerated.

This is not an abstract philosophical point. Courts in multiple jurisdictions have recognized the legitimacy of dignity-based prohibitions. Germany's constitutional framework explicitly balances free expression against human dignity, and the European Court of Human Rights has upheld restrictions on expression that degrades vulnerable groups. The Canadian Supreme Court, in R. v. Sharpe (2001), upheld the criminalization of certain forms of fictional child pornography precisely because of the attitudinal harm such material poses to children as a group, even when no real child was directly involved in its creation.

The same reasoning extends to ultra-realistic torture simulations. A virtual experience designed to allow users to enjoy the suffering of a realistic human being—to hear their screams, see their pain responses, and exercise deliberate cruelty upon them—is not a neutral act of imagination. It is a commodity built on the eroticization or gamification of human suffering, and its existence within a legal market sends an unmistakable social signal about the disposability of human pain.

III. The Inadequacy of the "No Victim, No Crime" Framework

The libertarian objection to criminalization typically reduces to a single claim: if no real person is harmed in the creation or consumption of the content, the state has no legitimate basis for prohibition. This argument, while superficially appealing, fails under scrutiny for several reasons.

First, it relies on an artificially narrow definition of "victim." If a pedophile uses AI-generated or artist-created VR simulations to groom a real child—showing them that "this is normal, look, it exists in virtual worlds too"—the child who is subsequently abused is a victim of a chain of events in which the simulated material played a material role. Law enforcement professionals have documented precisely this pattern with existing forms of virtual and computer-generated child exploitation material.

Second, the "no victim" framework ignores aggregate social harms. The widespread availability of such simulations creates communities of consumers whose shared engagement reinforces deviant norms, provides mutual validation, and lowers the collective threshold for escalation. This is not speculative sociology—it is the documented trajectory of online communities organized around child exploitation material, where researchers have consistently observed escalation patterns from "softer" to more extreme material over time.

Third, the argument proves too much. If the absence of a direct, identifiable victim were sufficient to immunize conduct from criminal sanction, we would be unable to justify laws against a wide range of offenses that virtually every legal system prohibits: conspiracy to commit crimes not yet executed, attempts that fail to reach completion, possession of certain weapons regardless of intent to use them, and—most relevantly—the possession of digitally altered images that depict realistic child sexual abuse. Many jurisdictions already criminalize computer-generated child sexual abuse material. Extending this prohibition to immersive VR simulations is not a radical expansion but a logical completion of existing legal principles applied to a more potent technological medium.

IV. Virtual Reality Is Categorically Different From Prior Media

A critical distinction must be drawn between VR simulations and prior forms of media that have depicted illegal acts. Novels, films, and video games have long portrayed murder, torture, and sexual violence without being subject to blanket criminalization. Why should VR be treated differently?

The answer lies in the nature of the medium itself. A novel about crime is filtered through language, abstraction, and the reader's imaginative interpretation. A film presents a third-person observation of actors performing scripted events. Even violent video games, while interactive, maintain clear aesthetic and mechanical barriers that remind the user of their artificiality—health bars, respawn mechanics, cartoonish physics.

Cutting-edge VR obliterates these mediating layers. The user does not read about, watch, or control an avatar who commits an act. The user commits the act themselves, with full sensory immersion, haptic feedback, spatial presence, and first-person embodiment. The psychological distance between simulation and reality collapses toward zero. This is not a difference of degree from prior media; it is a difference of kind. And differences of kind warrant different legal treatment.

When the act being simulated with this degree of fidelity is the sexual violation of a child, or the deliberate, sadistic torture of a human being, the argument that this is merely "another form of expression" equivalent to a passage in a Dostoevsky novel becomes untenable. The experiential reality of the simulation demands that the law recognize it as occupying a fundamentally different category.

V. Legal Precedent Supports Targeted Prohibition

Importantly, the criminalization being argued for here is not a broad censorship regime. It is a targeted prohibition of specific categories of content defined by their subject matter (child sexual abuse, realistic torture) and their medium (immersive, hyper-realistic virtual reality). This targeted approach is consistent with how democratic societies have always balanced free expression against competing values.

The United States, despite its exceptionally strong First Amendment protections, has consistently held that obscenity is not protected speech, that child pornography occupies a category subject to prohibition regardless of artistic merit, and that "true threats" and incitement may be criminally sanctioned. The PROTECT Act of 2003 criminalized computer-generated images indistinguishable from real child pornography—a direct precedent for extending prohibition to VR simulations that achieve comparable realism through immersive technology.

The United Kingdom's Coroners and Justice Act 2009 criminalized possession of prohibited images of children, including those that are entirely computer-generated, recognizing that the harm of such material is not contingent on the involvement of a real child in its production. Australia, Canada, and numerous European nations maintain similar provisions.

These legal frameworks reflect a mature democratic judgment: that certain categories of content are so fundamentally threatening to the welfare of the most vulnerable members of society that their prohibition is justified even at some cost to expressive freedom. The extension of these frameworks to cover immersive VR simulations is not a departure from democratic principle but its faithful application to new technological realities.

VI. The Therapeutic Objection Addressed

Some may argue that virtual simulations could serve a therapeutic purpose—allowing individuals with pedophilic urges to "safely" express them without harming real children. This argument should be treated with extreme caution for several reasons.

The clinical evidence does not support the "catharsis" model of deviant behavior. The overwhelming consensus among researchers who study sexual offending is that exposure to sexual material involving children reinforces and strengthens deviant arousal patterns rather than dissipating them. The catharsis hypothesis, drawn from outdated Freudian hydraulic models of emotion, has been largely discredited in contemporary psychology in favor of conditioning and social learning models that predict escalation, not satisfaction.

Moreover, even if a hypothetical therapeutic application were identified, it could be narrowly regulated through clinical oversight—much as controlled substances with therapeutic applications are available by prescription but prohibited for recreational use. The existence of a possible clinical use case does not justify the legal availability of such simulations to the general public.

VII. A Moral Society Must Draw Lines

Ultimately, the question of whether to criminalize hyper-realistic VR simulations of child sexual abuse and sadistic torture is a question about what kind of society we choose to be. Every legal system is an expression of moral commitments. Every criminal code draws lines that reflect a community's judgment about which forms of conduct are incompatible with the common good.

A society that permits the commercial creation and consumption of immersive experiences designed to simulate the rape of children is a society that has made a moral choice—and it is the wrong one. The fact that the child in the simulation is not "real" does not redeem the act of creating an entire experiential architecture devoted to making child rape pleasurable. The fact that the tortured person in the simulation is not "real" does not redeem the act of building a product designed to cultivate enjoyment of human suffering.

The law need not wait for perfect certainty about downstream effects to recognize that certain forms of conduct are intolerable on their face. We do not permit public displays of extreme obscenity and then demand proof that a specific viewer committed a specific subsequent offense before acknowledging the legitimacy of prohibition. We recognize that some boundaries are constitutive of a decent society—that their maintenance is not an infringement on freedom but a precondition of it.

Conclusion

The criminalization of hyper-realistic virtual reality simulations depicting child sexual abuse and sadistic torture is justified on multiple, reinforcing grounds: the neurological and psychological evidence of behavioral conditioning; the protection of human dignity; the documented patterns of normalization and escalation in communities that consume exploitative material; the categorical difference between immersive VR and prior media forms; and the extensive legal precedent for targeted prohibition of content that threatens society's most vulnerable members.

Technology does not alter moral reality. It amplifies it. The same imperative that drove societies to prohibit child sexual abuse material in photographic form, and subsequently in computer-generated form, now demands extension to the most immersive and psychologically potent medium yet created. To fail to act is not to preserve freedom—it is to abandon the most fundamental obligation of any legal system: the protection of those who cannot protect themselves, and the preservation of the moral foundations upon which all other freedoms depend.
